title: Globalization & Business Ethics Adventure 3: Market Entry & Ethics
welcome_lead: Today you'll choose a market entry method and weigh ethical dilemmas in international business.
meta_desc: Business Management: market entry methods (export, licensing, franchising, JV, subsidiary) and global ethics.
final_note: You compared five market entry methods and identified key ethical issues abroad.

concepts.def: Granting rights to use IP for a fee
Selling brand + system to local owner

walkthroughs.body_html:
Risk and commitment rise as a firm moves up the ladder.

1. Exporting — low risk, low control.
2. Licensing — IP fee; little oversight.
3. Franchising — brand and system shared (McDonald's, Subway).
4. Joint venture — local partner brings knowledge; profits split.
5. Wholly-owned subsidiary — full control, full risk.

Choice depends on host risk, control needs, capital, knowledge gap.

India and China often require joint ventures; the EU allows easy subsidiaries; emerging frontier markets may start with exports.

Issues: child labour, sweatshops, bribery (UK Bribery Act 2010, US FCPA), environmental dumping, tax avoidance.

Tools: codes of conduct, supplier audits, third-party certification, transparent supply chains (e.g. UK Modern Slavery Act 2015).

mcqs.q: How does HRM differ from traditional personnel management?
options: Manufacturing is in the tertiary sector along with services.

mcqs.q: Which sector does manufacturing belong to?
options: Manufacturing is in the primary sector because it makes things.
Manufacturing is in the tertiary sector along with services.
The secondary sector — which transforms raw materials from the primary sector (farming, mining) into finished goods.
